lines: Picture the exact same aggregation, built two completely different ways under the hood.
Does the engine's own cleanup process notice any difference between them at all?
Build that aggregation out of everyday, ordinary objects, the way you'd write it without thinking twice.
Run it, and the engine genuinely has to pay a real cost cleaning up afterward. Not nothing. A real, measurable cost.
Now build that exact same aggregation a different way, using the engine's own compact, purpose-built row format instead.
Does the engine still pay that same cleanup cost, or does something change?
steps.answer: The cost drops to almost nothing.

lines: Here's exactly what happens.
The compact-row version of that identical aggregation pays no measurable cleanup cost at all.
Not a smaller number. Genuinely nothing worth measuring.
Here's why that happens.
Cleanup cost tracks how many separate little pieces there are for the engine to sort through.
The compact row format was built specifically to need far fewer of those pieces in the first place.
Here's a different kind of question. That first version really did make the engine pay a real cleanup cost.
Does that mean cleanup is actually the thing slowing that job down?
steps.answer: No. It's real, but it's tiny next to how long the whole job took.

lines: Here's the measurement, laid out plainly.
That cleanup cost, while genuinely real, turns out to be a tiny sliver of the job's own total running time.
Nowhere close to being what's actually dragging that job down.
Here's the reasoning behind that.
A real, nonzero cleanup cost doesn't automatically mean trouble on its own.
It only tells you something once you put it next to how much total time the whole job actually spent running.
Put both versions' own numbers side by side: the same work, the same data.
One version pays a real cleanup cost. The other pays nothing worth measuring at all.
So how a piece of work gets built underneath decides how much cleanup it actually costs the engine.
And a real, nonzero cleanup number only means something once you've measured it against the whole job's own time.
